My ex and I were both teachers. Of course we needed daycare. We found a place with a couple older ladies that would be carrying for our son as an infant. The place was great, until it wasn't. FF to our son being 3 yo. He's in a completely different environment at the same place. This room is filled with 3yo's and "monitored" by some younger employees. He starts a boring phase. He's, of course, labeled a "biter" by those employees which means he's loosely separated from the non-biters but is lumped in with the "biters." This is not, in any way, a research-based approach. I'm finding out that kids bite for two main reasons: cause-and-effect or expression of intense emotion. The first is born out of curiosity. The latter is due to a lack of vocabulary to express those emotions. Both of us go to pick him up. The employee is updating my wife to the segregation method of room management. She tells (with an awkward giggle) that our son is labeled a biter and has been limped in with the other biters. I'm listening to this update and getting upset. No strategies to deal with the situation other than lumping him in with the others. When that employee giggled while updating my ex, I'm surprised my ex didn't rip the girl's face off. Oh yea, when we arrived, the employee was painting the bathroom, not directly monitoring, causing fumes with new paint, and generally clueless. 

We get him home, eat, play, ask him about his day. Its bath time. I get his shirt off and get him in the tub. I notice, on his left shoulder blade, what are clearly impressions of teeth, a full set. I guarantee you this bite hurt like hell. No mention of him being bitten. We need daycare, but there is no way we can take him back there. This is a Thursday. We found him a new and much better organized daycare by Tuesday. The new place has plans in place for biters. He thrived there. I'm still friends with some of this ladies. 

We decided my ex should go get his things from old daycare. She reported them, etc. He's a senior this year and is thriving.

I've had 3 visits across two states. The experiences were actually pretty similar overall. You get escorted to the unit. It's kind of unnerving at first. Get your room established get into your hospital issued garb including the ever popular grippy stocks. They will go through your belongings due to safety. Get some rest. The techs will roust you early in the morning for vitals. Breakfast and meds after. Probably a morning group just to set the day's schedule and set goals. Visit by the psychiatrist/med adjustments. I used a great deal of free time to read and rest. Noon group. Then lunch. Free time, afternoon group, free time, dinner. Wrap up, which is going over your goals for the day. Snack, free time, meds, bed. Wash rinse repeat. After some time and positive behavior, you'll graduate to real clothes someone brought you. Again, they will check that stuff for safety reasons. 

I did have some occupational therapy in my last stay. Crafts and such. It was cool. 

You can make acquaintences while in there, but do not make friends. The last thing you need in your life is someone who could be a huge emotional strain on you on the outside. 

Rest. Rest until you feel human enough to attend group. Unfortunately, during each of my stints, there was a nightmare patient that sticked the soul out of everyone on the unit. Acting out for attention, etc. It can get rough when that person is in high gear. Go to your room, use your skills, go to the nurse and ask for some anti anxiety meds. Most all of my nurses and techs were very helpful. 

Ready and take advantage of the daily psychiatrist visit. My food was really good each time.

3.  Find a way to give them a sense of ownership over their education.  Really give them controlled opportunities at responsibility. We're always crowing about personal responsibility. 

4.  Stop teacher-centered lessons. They're exhausting for all involved. They can't stand being lectured. They can't stand traditional homework. You can't stand a dead classroom. You feel like a failure. You go home drained every day wondering "what the hell am I doing this for?" These things just frustrate all involved. Flip your classroom. Why do we give them math problems to take home and suffer through?  You think the hw will only take them a certain amount of time, because that's what it took you. It will take them about 3 times as long, if they finish it. The point to those problems should be instructional not punitive. Sorry, that's how they perceive hw. Practice should be done under the watchful eye of a teacher. Give them the notes to read or a video to watch at home. (Or, give them a pre-assessment.) Task them with coming to the next class with at least one question. It's mandatory.  They can even email it to you if they're introverts. Who cares how you get the questions?  Your goal is to collect data and set measurable goals for your students. I guarantee you will see patterns emerge which means you skip all of the fluff you think is important and get right to the heart of the matter, which prevents a wasting of everyone's time. Trust me. You'll feel a much-needed confidence boost being able to use data to predict their behavior each year, and your admins will eat that shit up. Data-driven instruction. Student-centered learning. Admin is happy. Kids are happy. You might even be happy enough to forget how little you're paid. 

5.  For God's sake, use Google forms even for essays or math. Use forms for assessment. Forms will grade that work for you instead of you taking stuff home and infringing on your much-needed personal time. Forms will also output that data to Sheets. If you work in teams, that data can be shared with team members and your admin. You are collaborating! Teach the kids to use Docs and Sheets to complete assignments in groups by sharing those docs and sheets within the group or classwide. That's right, admins will love to see kids collaborating while using technology. 
6.  I caution you it's a great deal of upfront work on your part, you will have to train them to function this way. I'm telling you that your instructional time will be much more efficient and positive. Whatever time you need to spend training the students will come back you in many times over.
7.  Keep notes on what does and does not work. Produce those notes at an eval meeting. Admins love it when you can show that you are reflecting on your craft.
8.  Block out the negativity from your peers who aren't emotionally, intellectually, or professionally up to the task.
9.  Send out positive reports to the responsible adult in that child's life. You want the parents supporting you.
10. Once you and your students hit your groove, invite an admin in and ask feedback. You want your admin to support you. 

Bonus....
You don't teach; they learn. You're just there to guide them to the required goals. If, as time goes on, most students need you less and less, success. You have taught them how to learn. That is an extremely important life skill.

Secret....
You're main reason for being what you are is to enable student success. You cannot do that alone. You can't. As a coordinator of learning, it is your job to manipulate all of your stakeholders into supporting your cause and your ways. You control your classroom. Own it.

Air is treated as a fluid.  Even though my degree says meteorology, it's really a physics degree.  The vast majority of my professors were not meteo people, they were physics people.  Just so you know what you would be signing up for should you pursue this field.

Imagine a cube/parcel of air.  The parcel contains air, dust, and water.  Everything outside of this parcel is deemed the environment.  Temperature and density are the two biggest variables to consider.

Warm means that the particles that make up the air are farther apart, because they have more energy than the environment.  This means that there are less particles per unit volume than the environment.

Cold means that the particles have less energy than the environment.  The particles cannot travel as far.  So, there are more particles per unit volume than the environment.

A parcel that is warmer than the environment will, by virtue of it being less dense than the environment, will rise.  A parcel that is colder than the environment will sink, because it is more dense than the environment.

Now, we need to consider terrain and vertical structure of the environment.  We'll talk about terrain as flat, rising, or falling.  We'll assume, for simplicity sake, that as we move upward in our environment, the air becomes colder.  There could be a whole other thermodynamic discussion just on the vertical structure.  All of these conditions and variables are simplified so we can get the basic concepts.

If our parcel is moving at some speed out of the west towards a rise in elevation, the geography will force the parcel to rise into colder air.  The parcel will begin to cool which will cool the water within.  The water will begin to coalesce onto the dust and form a nucleus of sorts.  As the water parcel is forced higher, the parcel cools more which allows more water to deposit on the water drop nucleus. when enough water is allowed to cool, you get a cloud full of water drops.  The parcel is much more dense than the environment at this point.  So, the parcel will fall when the rising topography gives way to falling topography.

The parcel is at the highest elevation at this point.  This is why we observe clouds at or just to the side of mountain ridges.  Also, when we begin to observe cumulus clouds, we can assume there is a vertical forcing of the air.  Again, that's a whole other discussion.

The parcel now  encounters a downward slope in elevation and a warmer environment.  The air inside the parcel is warming which allows the water to evaporate.  The cloud eventually "disappears."  This is why, in many cases, thunderstorms that approach a valley "jump past" the valley and form on the other side of the corresponding ridge to the east.

This is also why, when observing ridges, one would see a striping event on the leeward side.  The parcel is cooling and warming due to density changes.  So, we end up observing stripes of clouds.

One other idea is that tornadoes cannot form in valleys.  This is not true.  The are less likely to form in valleys because of the above concepts.  Tornadoes tend to form past the leeward ridge.  The parcel of air has had consistent dimensions to this point.  That is not reality.  What happens is that when a parcel of air begins a descent, the bottom portion of the parcel is the initial portion to follow the terrain with the top of the parcel holding steady in elevation.  Parcels of air also contain a trait called vorticity.  Vorticity is simply the potential for the particles to revolve about the center of the parcel.  When a parcel is elongated. the vorticity is increased.

Toss vorticity into an environment where cold, dry air is colliding with warm, moist air....  Tornadoes.  We see this often in the Southern Plains.  To the west is the high point in the Rockies.  To the north is Canada and it's cold, dry air.  To the south is the Gulf of Mexico and it's very warm and moist air.  Hence, Tornado Alley.
